chunks: "An analog signal is continuous: at any instant it can take any value in a range, like the voltage from a microphone or a temperature sensor.
A digital signal is discrete: it only takes values from a finite set, usually just two, high and low, and it only changes or is only read at specific times.
You get from one to the other with an ADC.
It samples the analog signal at regular intervals, so time becomes discrete, and then quantizes each sample into one of 2 to the N levels, so amplitude becomes discrete.
A 12-bit converter with a 3. 3 volt range has 4096 levels, each about 0. 8 millivolts. That rounding adds quantization noise, about LSB over root twelve rms.
The big reason we like digital is noise immunity.
As long as noise stays within the noise margin, the receiver still decodes the right bit, and every gate regenerates a clean level, so noise doesn't accumulate along the chain.
Digital data can also be stored perfectly, copied, compressed, error-corrected and processed with flexible software.
The trade-offs: digital needs bandwidth and conversion hardware, has quantization error and latency, and sampling can alias if you violate Nyquist.
And I'd add that digital signals are really analog underneath: real logic edges have finite rise time, ringing and noise, and signal integrity problems are analog problems."
